NIDA’s Traveling Road Show "Understanding Drug Abuse" By Michael D. Cutler, Esq.

Michael D. Cutler, Esq., cutlermj@aol.com has been a trial attorney for 25 years, specializing for the last three years on drug policy as co-chair of NORML's amicus curiae subcommittee of its national legal committee, filing and helping to coordinate appellate briefs in cases from Washington state to Florida; and more recently, serving as national coordinator for the Voluntary Committee of Lawyers, seeking to organize lawyers to mainstream Drug War dissent, using a model of an attorney group originally formed to support the repeal of Alcohol Prohibition.
See Important and Outrageous Cases.

On April 2, 1998 in Boston MA, I attended the Al Leshner Show, also known as Understanding Drug Abuse and Addiction, Myths vs. Reality, A Town Meeting sponsored by: NIDA; Join Together (a project of Boston University's School of Public Health); the Mass. Dept. of Public Health's Bureau of Substance Abuse Services; the MA Governor's Alliance Against Drugs; City of Boston Substance Abuse Services; various graduate divisions of Brandeis Univ., Harvard Univ. and Boston College; McLean Hospital, and WGBH-TV (in conjunction with the Moyers' PBS-TV series: Addiction, Close to Home).  While I have a bias, I have used {To insert my more pejorative comments}.

The Program Content

This road show has appeared in at least four other American cities, but the attendance in Boston, at over 500, was described as the largest turnout by far. The program consisted of introductory remarks by among others, the state Public Health Commissioner and the Mayor of the City of Boston, followed by a keynote address NIDA director Leshner.
SeeThe Scientist Magazine Does A Reverent Interview with the Head of NIDA .

He in turn was followed by the former state public health commissioner Mulligan on the implications of drug abuse trends in Massachusetts. Next was a series of panelists on the issues of using statistics to develop local prevention plans; behavioral modification therapy for addicts; and, the influence of managed care on drug abuse treatment services.

After lunch the so-called town meeting was convened, actually eight sessions for randomly selected groups of the 500 conference participants (mine contained about 30-40 attendees) for an hour, moderated by a Join Together staff person, two "conversation starters" and a NIDA staff person. The last event was a series of workshops: I attended Understanding Drugs and the Brain, featuring a Harvard Medical School and McLean Hospital Ph.D. Associate in Psychiatry, who presented "Marihuana Effects on Brain and Behavior."

The Message and the Audience

The main message, espoused by virtually all speakers with frequent reference to the Moyers PBS Addiction series, was to educate the public, including private health insurers, medical care providers and legislative and other public funders, that addiction and drug abuse were diseases, for which there existed scientifically-based effective treatments, far more successful and less expensive than simple aversive criminal justice "treatment" through incarcerating drug users. The audience consisted primarily of treatment providers, all looking for more money, either from state or local government, or from NIDA.

The conference's bottom line was that all attendee providers deserved more money to expand the availability of drug treatment on demand for all who needed it, regardless of an ability to pay. {Of course, the Gorilla in the hall that everyone ignored [except yours truly] was the Drug War, and its consumption [by the criminal justice system] of four times the resources available for treatment}. Few spoke seriously about how to grow the treatment side of the fiscal pie, only that it ought to grow. Exceptions were tobacco control advocates, who advocated funding treatment from increasing taxes on tobacco and alcohol consumers {As regressive a tax as the state lottery.} Also, some urged the expansion of private insurance benefits, to cover more effective and longer terms of treatment, including provision for multiple relapse treatment.

The Local Celebrity

Mayor Tom Menino is popular, having been reelected without opposition. He is as common-folk and non-elitist a politician as his predecessor, Ray Flynn our latest Vatican ambassador. While Flynn sees (and condemns) the Drug War's consequences on people of color and few assets, however, Menino does not "get it," except to understand that treatment is more cost effective than incarceration. In working for a "Drug-free Boston," the Mayor supported the criminal justice system's vital role in deterring drug use, but was "not the only answer." Treatment programs were appropriate to "help the mistake makers," rather than allowing them to be "cut out of society."

The City's drug czarina, a deeply religious black woman, also spoke. She is a fervent 12-stepper who believes the cure for drug abuse will be found in the Almighty more than mere mortals. She expressed strong opposition to both the moral and punitive response to drug addiction. {She sees the problem as focused on drugs, however, rather than Prohibition.}

NIDA Director Leshner

Leshner is quite affable on the stump, although given his financial hold on the futures of most audience members, they could not fawn enough regardless of what he said. Trust Us Scientists, Leshner promised; the police and the prisons will hold onto the patients, so we can cure them. "We know we have many effective tools in the clinical toolbox, many of which have been tested scientifically. Now the task is to use them. . . . There is more and more advocacy for treatment while people are in prison. The advocates are the criminal justice people {The CJS wants ALL the money, for punitive AND NON-punitive responses to drug use.}''

Equating use and addiction, Leshner expressed the need for complex solutions for the damage caused by drugs {Ignoring Prohibition}, requiring complex NIDA research (Ed.: And of course, bigger NIDA budgets; Leshner has presided over a massive increase in NIDA funding, Clinton's favorite supplement to prison funding). Leshner paid lip-service to the Physicians' Leadership advocacy of treating addiction as a treatable illness, but distinguished drug users (not only abusers) from coffee and tobacco addicts, because of drugs' brain-damaging effects {As demonstrated by NIDA's unique brand of politically-driven science}.

Leshner closed with the point identified by Physicians Leadership, that there is a "disconnection" between the "reality" of the effectiveness of drug treatment, and the "myth" of the public's perception, that aversive incarceration "therapy" is the best way to cure drug use {Remember, Leshner does not distinguish use from abuse, or addiction for that matter}. Recalling the public's former intolerance for and stigmatization of mental illness, Leshner called on the audience to help bridge the gap between scientific reality and public myth about drug treatment.

I tried to frame a question seeking Leshner's comment on seeking increased treatment funding by reducing the criminal justice side of the spending pie, identifying the decriminalization of adult marijuana use as an appropriate way to do so, given that the addictive quality of cannabis was well below legal drugs like alcohol and tobacco according to NIDA's own research (the Henningfield and Benowitz studies of 1994).
See The Relative Addictiveness of Drugs According to NIDA's Own Researcher

Leshner denied that NIDA ever studied the relative addictive qualities of drugs, then reiterated that drug use is bad and he does not distinguish between use and addiction. Regarding the growth of the treatment slice at the expense of the criminal justice slice of the funding pie, he explained such advocacy was not NIDA's job, but "yours" (referring to the audience).

Other Policy Speakers

Soon after Leshner finished, former state public health commissioner Mulligan spoke directly to the need to increase the treatment response and reduce the punitive response to drug abuse. {While an opponent of recreational marijuana use, Mulligan has been outspoken in support of medicinal marijuana, having witnessed its benefits with a close acquaintance. His speech did not mention medicinal marijuana.} The local trends include an increase in heroin use, an increase in adolescent marijuana use and reduced funding for intensive out-patient drug treatment. Mulligan urged lobbying to transfer public funds from the criminal justice response to non-violent drug use, to the more cure-effective and cost-effective treatment response. Adapting Leshner's "we have the tools" to treat drug users analogy, Mulligan criticized the lack of funds to put those tools to use.

One of the more interesting policy speeches covered the impact of managed care programs on drug treatment. Such programs now consume $3B annually in premiums and expenses. Barriers to insurance coverage in the past have included patients' stigmatization and denial, and the insurers' perceptions that drug abuse resulted in extraordinary patient impairment and service consumption. Promising trends appeared, however, in "carve-out" plans, where mental health and drug treatment services were managed and funded by a program separate from the provision of other insured health services. Using carve-out specialists focusing on swift and brief non-judgmental intervention, utilization rates were shown to be within normal limits of non-mental health rates, and in-patient treatment utilization and its dramatically inflated costs were significantly reduced.

The Town Meeting

Among the initial speakers at my rump caucus, the interactive feature of the conference with a NIDA witness present, was a local police chief who described his suburb as in denial of its drug abuse problems. Although described as a forum for relating what worked and did not work, so NIDA could more accurately focus its funding,  the first attendee to speak was Dr. Janet Lapey,, of Drug Watch International {A Flat Earth Hall of Famer}. She encouraged all to buy the latest Readers Digest
(See

I arose later, to reply to Lapey. I suggested that the attendance of adolescents using marijuana at protest rallies was evidence of the failure of drug prohibition as the nation's only drug strategy. I tried to express common cause with treatment providers, urging that the only way to fund treatment on demand was to reduce the criminal justice slice of the pie, by slicing out adult marijuana use from the criminal justice plate (the conference lunch had just ended). I attempted to suggest, in concert with the intended purpose of the session as sharpening NIDA's research focus, that NIDA study European drug control experience, citing Holland, Spain and Switzerland.

Lapey popped up, brandishing the October 1997 Science magazine article on the MacCoun and Reuter study of Holland (conveniently included in the program materials by NIDA), for the conclusion {Not supported by the article's authors} that cannabis legalization inevitably causes the proliferation of marijuana use by adolescents. I answered that Dutch rates of youthful use were still below ours, and that the authors had noted a similar or greater rise in the rate of American youth use over the same period despite Prohibition. The audience appeared to react with comments about what a "zoo" Europe was and {Despite statistics to the contrary}, how much worse their hard drug problems have become {Still far below ours}.
See Comparison of drug addiction levels in various European countries.

Marijuana's Brain Damage.

My last program of the day drove me out of the conference in a tizzy (I have a low tizzy threshold). In a slick light show of CAT scan brain photos, laser pointers and ragged line graphs, Ph.D. Elena Kouri almost convinced me that by now, I must be severely retarded. According to Kouri, what makes cannabis intoxicating and a natural pest repellent is its dysfunctional impact on the insect nervous system. Naturally, human nervous systems are similarly at risk. With unconscious analogy to Morgan and Zimmer, Kouri identified several marijuana "myths and realities."

"Myth": Marijuana leaves no residual effect. "Reality": Her test subjects (5000 intoxicating experiences, equivalent to a daily high for 14 years; not me) displayed permanent alteration of their central nervous systems. "Permanent impact" turned out to be a weakened ability to sort playing cards 24 hours after intoxication, with an admission that more testing {And NIDA grant money} was necessary to show harmful results over longer duration's.

"Myth": Marijuana is not addictive; in "reality", the suddenly abstinent 14 year user suffers withdrawal symptoms such as sleep disorder, anxiety and appetite change, although these symptoms were admittedly "more subtle" than the symptoms of cocaine withdrawal. Because self-reporting of aggressive withdrawal symptoms "didn't work" {No aggression reported}, a test was devised using a computer game where the test subject could add points to his score or subtract points from his computer competitor (deemed evidence of aggression). On abstinence days 3 and 4 (but at no other time), the "withdrawing" marijuana (ab)users showed increased competitor point subtraction, and hence, anti-social aggression {I did not make up this report}.

Conclusion

NIDA's support for Moyers' conclusion, that addiction treatment is cheaper and more effective than incarceration, is useful to reducing (somewhat) the harm caused by current drug policy. Similarly, NIDA appears willing to support research and programming to change public perception, to overcome public hostility to drug treatment by showing it to be a better response to drug use than imprisonment. Since marijuana pro(per)secution remains a lynch-pin of drug prohibition, however, NIDA remains heavily invested in any research that in anyway demonstrates that cannabis is more harmful than water. Further, its refusal to adopt a position on the relative harms of drugs, and its failure to distinguish between adult use and abuse or addiction, clearly place NIDA as part of the problem of drug prohibition, rather than a means to the reduction of drug abuse.
